Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced BOCRA (national telecoms regulator) records of a 2025 regulator-driven mobile tariff review that cut Mascom, Orange and BTC data prices by 15-30%, plus 2026 bundle restructuring (e.g. BTC 30GB for P199/30 days). Older ITU ICT Price Basket data (2016-2018) put Botswana at 7-12% of GNI per capita for a comparable basket, but no post-2025 figure computed to the ITU basket methodology (cheapest plan with minimum 2GB, 30-day validity) was located. A rough calculation using current bundle prices and 2024 GNI per capita (USD7,750, World Bank) suggests the current cost is likely under 2% of monthly GNI per capita, but this is an approximation rather than a verified ITU/A4AI statistic. Flagged for human review to confirm against the precise basket methodology rather than assert an upgraded code on an approximation.
revised_comments: Botswana's mobile network operators (Mascom, Orange, BTC) implemented regulator-mandated data tariff cuts of 15-30% in 2025 following a BOCRA costing and pricing study, with further bundle restructuring in early 2026 (for example BTC's 30-day bundles of 30GB for P199). Historical ITU ICT Price Basket data placed the cost of a comparable mobile data basket at around 7-12% of monthly GNI per capita in 2016-2018, a figure BOCRA's intervention was explicitly designed to reduce. A precise current percentage-of-GNI figure calculated to ITU's basket methodology is not available.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The light check surfaced a BOCRA (Botswana's telecoms regulator) 2021 Broadband Facts and Figures report giving raw international bandwidth capacity (incoming ~107,860 Mbps, of which 56,475 Mbps/52% utilised, as at June 2021), more current and authoritative than generic search results, so the row moved to the full path. However, ITU's own published 'international bandwidth per Internet user' statistic for Botswana (via TheGlobalEconomy.com, sourced to ITU) last reports only 16.44 kbit/s per user in 2016 (range 6.44-16.44 kbit/s, 2012-2016), which would score 2 (Low). Deriving a current per-user figure from the 2021 BOCRA capacity data requires assumptions about internet-user numbers that are not reliably available (World Bank/ITU internet-user percentage series for Botswana are inconsistent across sources: variously cited as 73.5%, 75.2%, 77.3% and 78.7% for 2021-2022, versus Statistics Botswana's own 2024 household survey reporting only 57.5% internet use). Given this inconsistency and the lack of a directly-reported recent ITU per-user bandwidth statistic, the code cannot be confidently recalculated. Flagged for human review rather than asserting a code from an approximation.
revised_comments: Botswana's international internet bandwidth is provided through the state-backed wholesaler BoFiNet together with private carriers (Seacom, Liquid Intelligent Technologies, Paratus Telecom, BTC), sourcing capacity via South African and Namibian transit routes and submarine cable landing points, as Botswana itself is landlocked. BOCRA's 2021 Broadband Facts and Figures report recorded total incoming international bandwidth of approximately 107,860 Mbps (52% utilised) and outgoing bandwidth of approximately 98,497 Mbps (8% utilised), continuing a multi-year upward trend. A standardised international-bandwidth-per-internet-user figure comparable to ITU's methodology is not currently available.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check found Packet Clearing House (PCH), the primary directory named in the search hint, listing an active Botswana Internet Exchange (BINX) in Gaborone, established October 2005 and managed by the Botswana Internet Exchange association. This is a direct hit on the recommended primary source, so the row was moved from the fast to the full path. PCH's own record notes 'work is happening, still need to sort out formalities' and shows no populated subnet/participant data in its public listing, while AFRINIC/PeeringDB records confirm at least one participant (Botswana Fibre Networks/BoFiNet, AS37678) peering at the exchange. This indicates a single, still-maturing IXP with limited (rather than broad) participation, corresponding to a score of 3 rather than 4 or 5.
revised_comments: Botswana has a single operational Internet Exchange Point, the Botswana Internet Exchange (BINX), based in Gaborone and established in 2005, listed as active in the Packet Clearing House global IXP directory. Participation is limited: AFRINIC and PeeringDB records show at least one major network (Botswana Fibre Networks/BoFiNet) peering at the exchange, but PCH's own administrative notes describe governance formalities as still being finalised, and detailed subnet/traffic data is not publicly published, indicating a single IXP with limited participation rather than a mature, broadly-subscribed exchange.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced Botswana Power Corporation (BPC)-sourced retail tariff data (via GlobalPetrolPrices, September 2025: BWP1.267/kWh residential, ~USD0.095/kWh) and a BERA (Botswana Energy Regulatory Authority) public notice confirming BPC's current domestic tariff and a pending 46% average increase for 2026-27 (moving domestic tariff from P0.90 to P1.57/kWh, weighted average P1.56 to P2.28/kWh). Both are primary, authoritative sources named in the search hint, so the row moved to the full path. Estimating a basic residential consumption of roughly 100-150 kWh/month (a common 'lifeline' band) at the current BWP1.267/kWh tariff and Botswana's 2024 GNI per capita (USD7,750, World Bank) gives a cost of roughly 1.0-1.5% of monthly per-capita income, placing Botswana in the 'Affordable (1-2%)' band. This estimate is approximate since it is not a directly reported World Bank/ESMAP affordability statistic, and the approved 46% tariff rise due in 2026-27 will materially increase this share going forward.
revised_comments: Residential electricity in Botswana is supplied by the state utility, Botswana Power Corporation (BPC), and regulated by the Botswana Energy Regulatory Authority (BERA). As at September 2025, the residential tariff was BWP1.267 per kWh (approximately USD0.095), which for typical lifeline consumption levels represents roughly 1-2% of monthly GNI per capita, indicating electricity remains broadly affordable for residential consumers. However, BERA has approved a substantial tariff increase of up to 46% for the 2026-27 period (moving the domestic tariff from P0.90 to P1.57 per kWh), driven by BPC's reliance on imported power and unreliable local generation, which is expected to reduce affordability materially in the near term.

Definition: The maturity of the country's technology startup ecosystem, based on the number of tech startups, venture capital activity, accelerators/incubators, and the presence of a supportive ecosystem. Africa's startup scene is well-documented by trackers like Partech, Disrupt Africa, and Briter Bridges.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced substantial, recent (April 2026) coverage from Disrupt Africa, TechCabal and Mmegi Online of the newly-launched Botswana Tech Fund (BTF), a Guernsey-anchored multi-stage VC vehicle targeting GBP10m/USD64m in total commitments (first close GBP5m/USD6.7m), plus the government-backed Botswana Innovation Fund's new Scalar Botswana Innovation Programme for climate/digital startups. These are authoritative, named, dated sources directly matching the search hint (Disrupt Africa, TechCabal), so the row moved from fast to full path. TechCabal explicitly frames Botswana/Southern Africa (excluding South Africa) as receiving under a fifth of African VC funding, and BTF's disclosed first-close capital (~USD6.7m) falls well short of the USD50m/year threshold for 'Established'. Given a small number of active funding vehicles and hubs and limited disclosed deal flow to date, a score of 2 (Emerging) is the best-supported reading, though the direction of travel (new dedicated VC fund, government innovation programme) is a genuine and recent positive shift.
revised_comments: Botswana's tech startup ecosystem is at an early stage but has seen a notable recent catalyst: the April 2026 launch of the Botswana Tech Fund (BTF), a multi-stage venture capital vehicle anchored by British investor Stephen Lansdown's Pula Investments and advised by Launch Africa Ventures, targeting USD64m in total commitments with a first close of roughly USD6.7m, partnered with the Botswana Innovation Hub for deal sourcing and portfolio support. The government-backed Botswana Innovation Fund also runs dedicated startup support, including a 2026 twelve-month programme for climate and digital-technology startups. Disclosed venture capital funding to Botswana-based startups nonetheless remains modest by regional standards, with Southern African markets outside South Africa historically attracting under a fifth of all African VC funding.

Definition: The number and activity level of technology hubs, incubators, accelerators, and co-working spaces focused on technology and innovation. These provide physical infrastructure and support for tech entrepreneurship and skills development.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check found Botswana Innovation Hub (BIH, also known as Botswana Digital & Innovation Hub, BDIH) listed in the AfriLabs pan-African hub directory named in the search hint, plus the Institute of Entrepreneurial Development's (IED) Business Incubator/Venture Creation Labs. This is a legitimate authoritative hit (AfriLabs directory), so the row moved to the full path. Only two distinct hub organisations were identified with public evidence of active programming (BIH's science and technology park with tenant/incubation space, and IED's Venture Creation Labs incubator, which includes a women-focused co-working space). No evidence of 3 or more independently operating hubs was found, corresponding to a score of 2 (1-2 hubs with limited activity) rather than 3, though BIH has been operating since the mid-2000s with an active tenant base and a new link to the Botswana Tech Fund.
revised_comments: Botswana's technology and innovation hub landscape is concentrated around a small number of institutions. The principal hub is the Botswana Innovation Hub (also Botswana Digital & Innovation Hub), a government-backed science and technology park in Gaborone hosting ICT, biotechnology and energy-focused tenant companies, listed in the AfriLabs pan-African network of hubs and now partnered with the newly-launched Botswana Tech Fund for deal sourcing. A second identifiable hub is the Institute of Entrepreneurial Development's Business Incubator, which runs Venture Creation Labs, including a dedicated women's co-working and incubation space. Beyond these two anchor institutions, there is limited public evidence of additional independently operating technology hubs or accelerators in the country.

Definition: The proportion of the population with basic digital skills (ability to use a computer, smartphone, or the internet for simple tasks such as sending messages, finding information, or using apps). Based on ITU household survey data, Afrobarometer, or national ICT surveys.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced Statistics Botswana's own 2024 ICT Household Survey Stats Brief (published August 2025), a primary national statistical source directly matching the search hint, reporting that individuals with e-skills rose from 41.4% (556,688 people) in 2014 to 59.2% (1,071,314 people) in 2024, alongside 57.5% internet usage and 84.2% mobile phone usage. This is a clear, authoritative, country-specific and recent figure, so the row moved from fast to full path. The 59.2% e-skills figure falls within the 40-59% band on the variable's scale, corresponding to a score of 4.
revised_comments: Statistics Botswana's 2024 ICT Household Survey (published August 2025) found that 59.2% of individuals (1,071,314 people) had basic ICT/e-skills, up from 41.4% in 2014, alongside 57.5% internet usage and 84.2% mobile phone usage. This places basic digital literacy in the 40-59% band, reflecting a majority-digitally-literate but not yet universal population.
